q-75187.name: Question 1
q-75187.problem:
Which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=(x-4)({x}^{2}+3)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
q-75187.worked_solution:
The equation is already fully factored. Note that the discriminant of ${x}^{2}+3=0$ is 

$$
D=(0)^{2}-4(1)(3)=-12<0,
$$

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that the function $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=4.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by plugging the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(0-4)({0}^{2}+3) \\  & =(-4)(3) \\  & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve:

- has a $y$-intercept at the point $(0,-12),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=4,$ and

- has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14240558/assets/310ba3049a0a91f23259a67eb3c0606749f6a83a75151d6b0d41dfc4e98706d1.png)

q-112435.name: Question 3
q-112435.problem:
Given that $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x)=3{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}+x-3,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
q-112435.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x-3)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-3)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 3 & 3 & -9 & 1 & -3 \\  &  & 9 & 0 & 3 \\  & 3 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{f(x)}{x-3}=3{x}^{2}+1
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=(x-3)(3{x}^{2}+1).
$$

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of $3{x}^{2}+1=0$ is 

$$
D=(0)^{2}-4(3)(1)=-12<0,
$$

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=3.$ 

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3(0)^{3}-9(0)^{2}+0-3=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve:

- has a $y$-intercept at $(0,-3),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=3,$ and

- has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

q-112498.problem:
Given that $(x+3)$ is a factor of $f(x)=-4{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}-3x-9,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)

First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+3)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+3)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+3)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -3 & -4 & -12 & -3 & -9 \\  &  & 12 & 0 & 9 \\  & -4 & 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(x)}{x+3} & =-4{x}^{2}-3 \\  & =-(4{x}^{2}+3),\end{aligned}
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=-(x+3)(4{x}^{2}+3).
$$

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of $4{x}^{2}+3=0$ is 

$$
D=(0)^{2}-4(4)(3)=-48<0,
$$

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=-3.$ 

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
y=-4(0)^{3}-12(0)^{2}-3(0)-9=-9
$$

So, the curve:

- has a $y$-intercept at $(0,-9),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-3,$ and

- has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the graph has an $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:
